I just spent 3 months building an AI agent from scratch.

Everyone said to use a framework.

But here's the thing → frameworks hide the complexity.

They don't remove it.

I learned more in those 3 months than in 2 years of using LangChain.

Here's what actually matters:

→ Prompt engineering is 80% of the work
→ Memory management is harder than generation
→ Error handling is where agents actually break
→ Evaluation is still an unsolved problem

The frameworks will catch up.

But understanding the fundamentals won't go out of style.

Comment AGENT if you've built from scratch too.

Hot take: LinkedIn engagement is down 40% across the board.

But my posts are up 3x.

The difference? I stopped writing for the algorithm.

I started writing for 1 specific person in my audience.

Every post now answers ONE question that ONE person asked me that week.

That's it. No growth hacks. No engagement pods.

Just genuine answers to real questions.

We just hit 250K members across 200 chapters worldwide.

2 years ago we were 12 people in a Portland coffee shop.

I remember thinking 'if we can get to 100 members, we've made it.'

Now we're in 50 countries.

The secret? We never optimized for growth.

We optimized for the experience of showing up to your first event.

→ Every chapter has a local host
→ Every event has a theme
→ Every attendee gets a follow-up

Community scales when you make the smallest unit excellent.

Comment BUILD if you're growing a community too.

Whoa. Claude just got a major upgrade.

I've been testing it for 2 weeks as an Anthropic ambassador.

The coding capabilities are genuinely different.

Not incrementally better. Categorically different.

I gave it a bug that took my team 3 days to find.

It found it in 4 minutes. With a fix.

Here's what changed:

→ It actually reads your entire codebase now
→ It remembers context across long sessions
→ The tool use is reliable enough for production

We're past the 'cool demo' phase.

This is 'replace your junior dev's debugging workflow' phase.

Comment CLAUDE if you want me to share my testing notes.

I got rejected from Y Combinator.

Twice.

But here's why I'm grateful:

The first rejection forced me to talk to 200 customers.

The second rejection forced me to get profitable.

Both things YC would have told me to do anyway.

Except I did them without giving up 7% equity.

The best accelerator is a closed door and a burning need to prove someone wrong.

Not every rejection is redirection.

Some rejections are the accelerator.
